A B S T R A C T  
Designing a hole-transport material (HTM) that guarantees effective hole transport while self-assembling at the 
perovskite|HTM interface with the formation of an ordered interlayer, has recently emerged as a promising 
strategy for high-performance and stable perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Hydrogen bonding (HB) is a versatile 
multi-functional tool for the design of small molecular HTMs. However, to date, its employment is mostly limited 
to p-i-n inverted PSCs. This study demonstrates the advantages of a novel HTM design that can self-assemble into 
a long-range ordered interlayer on the perovskite surface via HB association. A hydro-functional HTM (O1) is 
compared to a reference HTM (O2) that cannot form HB due to the replacement of the amide group of O1 with a 
plain butyl alkyl chain in O2. As a result, O1-based n-i-p PSCs display enhanced hole extraction reaction, sup­
pressed interfacial charge recombination, reduced hysteresis effect, and an increase in Voc (by 60 mV), FF (>11% 
increase), and overall power conversion efficiency, PCE (32% increase) compared to the case of HB-free O2- 
based devices. Remarkable stability is observed for unencapsulated O1 cells, with a T80 lifetime of 35.5 h under 
continuous maximum power point tracking in air. This work emphasizes the role of HB-directed self-assembling 
in simultaneously enhancing both the PCE and stability of popular n-i-p PSCs. This study paves the way for the 
development of new hydro-functional charge-transport material designs for efficient and stable PSCs.

of the HTM with the realization of such a functional interlayer within the 
same molecule is undoubtedly beneficial for the interfacial transfer 
dynamics as well as for the protection of the perovskite layer against the 
degradation factors, such as the atmospheric moisture and hygroscopic 
dopants migration from the HTM’s side. To realize a well-defined 
interfacial functionalization, self-assembly via noncovalent in­
teractions has been recognized as one promising strategy for establish­
ing a long-range order of the small molecules at the interface [14–16]. 
Canil et al. constructed an interfacial self-assembled monolayer (SAM) 
with small dipolar molecules to achieve a controlled tuning of the 
perovskite work function [17]. Cai et al. reported a phenoxazine-based 
HTM, namely N01, functionalized with bromo-hexyl for the tuning of its 
self-assembling properties. The as-synthesized N01 self-assembles into 
an ordered lamellar structure via weak dipole-dipole interactions 
involving C–H⋅⋅⋅O, C–H⋅⋅⋅Br, and π–π interactions, which benefits the 
hole mobility, surface properties, and perovskite growth, eventually 
contributing to the achievement of high PCE (21.85%) for stable 
inverted PSCs [18]. Very recently, hydrogen bonding-associated self-­
assembly has been introduced in the design of new functionalized HTMs 
forming superstructures at the interface with perovskite [19]. 
Hydrogen bonding (HB) is a non-covalent electrostatically-driven 
interaction between a hydrogen atom and an electronegative atom 
bearing a lone pair of electrons, which can realize well-organized 
intermolecular or intramolecular nanostructures [20]. To date, the 
employment of hydrogen-bonded HTMs has been mainly limited to the 
fabrication of p-i-n inverted PSCs. Janssen’s group prepared inverted 
PSCs with hydrogen-bonded HTM based on azapolyheteroaromatic 
small molecules through a complex thermal evaporation technique due 
to the poor solubility of the HTM. The corresponding devices achieved 
the maximum PCE of 15.9% with a moderate device stability measured 
in a time scale of a few hundreds of seconds [19]. Instead of the small 
molecules, Hagfeldt’s group formed hydrogen-bonded NiOx nano­
particles as the inorganic HTM through ionic liquid-assisted synthesis, to 
construct p-i-n devices with a very high PCE of > 22%, which also 
demonstrates a high maximum power point tracking (MPPT) stability by 
retaining 92% of the initial PCE after 1000 h ageing of the encapsulated 
devices [21]. In our recent work, a lactam-based small molecule forming 
intramolecular HB upon thermal annealing contributed to the fabrica­
tion of high-performance inverted PSCs (PCE of champion device: 
21.62%), which can retain 87% of its initial performance (as encapsu­
lated devices) after 500 h MPPT test in N2 atmosphere. However, such a 
reliance on thermal annealing makes this approach unsuitable for n-i-p 
PSCs [20]. To the best of our knowledge, there are only two reported 
designs of hydrogen-bonded HTMs for n-i-p PSCs, both employing an 
amide group [22,23]. Nevertheless, in these examples the HB lies in the 
core of the amide units, hence impeding the realization of a long-range 
ordered interlayer above the perovskite surface. Therefore, designing a 
suitable hydrogen-bonded HTM that can self-assemble at the perovskite 
interface and boost the performance and ambient stability of n-i-p PSCs 
without encapsulation is highly desirable yet challenging. 
Herein, we designed a butanamide substituted carbazole (CA)-based 
material capped at both ends with electron-rich units of triphenylamine 
(TPA), namely O1 (Fig. 1a). O1 molecule exhibits good hole selectivity, 
energy levels alignment, and stability, while self-assembling into an 
ordered interfacial modifier for the perovskite surface via HB associa­
tion, i.e., N–H⋅⋅⋅O––C. We compare the results with O2 (Fig. 1b), a ma­
terial with a similar structure except for the replacement of butanamide 
by a plain butyl alkyl chain, i.e., not capable of HB formation. We 
demonstrate that the hole mobility of O1 increases by a factor of 3 
compared to that of O2 due to the formation of HB-associated supra­
molecular structures within the O1 HTM. The HB-directed self-assem­
bled interlayer at the interface of perovskite and O1 HTM significantly 
improves the hole extraction while effectively hindering the non­
radiative recombination. The employment of O1 HTM in n-i-p standard 
PSCs (highest PCE of 15.1%) leads to a distinct performance enhance­
ment of 32% compared to the case of HB-free O2 HTM. Our MPPT test 
for unencapsulated devices under continuous 1 sun illumination (100 
mW cm−2) in air, confirms the notably enhanced stability of O1 HTM- 
based devices with a T80 lifetime of 35.5 h, which is nearly one order

2.4. Fabrication of O1 and O2 HTMs-based CsFAMA PSCs 
CsFAMA-based PSCs were fabricated with a reported one-step 
method [24]. In a typical fabrication process, FTO glass substrates 
(2 cm × 2 cm) were wet chemically etched with 2 M HCl aqueous so­
lution and zinc powder. The etched FTO substrates were then sonicated 
using an aqueous Mucasol solution (2% in water), acetone, and 2-prop­
anol for 15 min in each step, successively. After swiftly drying with 
compressed dry air, the substrates were treated with UV-ozone for 
15 min to remove organic residuals and increase hydrophilicity. A 
~30 nm thick (determined by a surface profiler, Dektak 150 stylus 
profilometer) compact TiO2 layer (c-TiO2) was deposited on the 
as-prepared FTO substrate by spray pyrolysis of 0.38 M TDBA solution in 
2-propanol at 450 ◦C. The films were then sintered at 450 ◦C for 1 h in 
air. A mesoporous TiO2 (m-TiO2) scaffold layer was made by 
spin-coating an ethanolic suspension of 30NRD TiO2 nanoparticle paste 
(150 mg TiO2 paste in 1 mL ethanol) at 4000 rpm for 10 s. The films 
were quickly dried at 100 ◦C for 10 min prior to calcination at 450 ◦C for 
30 min under a continuous air flow. The films were then cooled down to 
150 ◦C and directly transferred into a nitrogen-filled glovebox. To make 
a ~500 nm thick CsFAMA perovskite film, the perovskite precursor 
comprised FAI (0.95 M), PbI2 (1.1 M), MABr (0.19 M), PbBr2 (0.2 M), 
and CsI (0.06 M) in a mixed solvent of DMF:DMSO (4:1, v-v). 50 µl so­
lution was spin-coated onto the as-prepared FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2 sub­
strate at 1000 rpm for 10 s, followed by 6000 rpm for 20 s 100 µl 
chlorobenzene was swiftly dropped as the anti-solvent treatment 5 s 
prior to the programming end. The perovskite layer was then annealed 
at 110 ◦C for 1 h. The resulting perovskite composition has a stoichi­
ometry of Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)0.95Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3, namely CsFAMA 
perovskite. After annealing, the doped O1- or O2-based HTM was 
dynamically spin-coated at 1800 rpm for 40 s on top of the as-formed 
perovskite layer. Four concentrations (5, 10, 20, 25 mg/mL, in chloro­
benzene) of O1-based HTM solutions were prepared to tune the HTM 
film thickness. The doped O1 or O2 solution (e.g., 20 mg/mL) was ob­
tained by first adding 20 mg O1 or O2 and 8 µl 4-tBP to 1 mL chloro­
benzene, which was stirred at 60 ℃ for 3 min. Then 4.8 µl Li-TFSI 
(520 mg/mL) and 8.1 µl FK209 (300 mg/mL) pre-dissolved in acetoni­
trile were added to the O1 or O2 solution, respectively. Finally, a 100 nm 
thick gold electrode was thermally evaporated in a high vacuum (5 ×
10−4 mbar) on top of the HTM layer.

interlayer on the device performance. Fig. 5a depicts the energy level 
diagram of a complete PSC with the structure ‘FTO|TiO2|CsFAMA|HTM|

effect of O1 thickness on the device performance was evaluated by 
changing the concentration of O1 (from 5 to 25 mg/mL in chloroben­
zene) in the spin-coating solution. The best PCE was achieved with a 
~95 nm thick O1 layer (determined in Fig. 5b) obtained from a con­
centration of 20 mg/mL (see the performance comparison in Table S8 in

average solar cell performance (15 pixels for each case) and the 
photovoltaic parameters of the champion devices (see the statistical 
analysis of the photovoltaic parameters in Figs. 5d-g). When comparing 
O1- and O2-based devices, a significantly improved Voc (1030 mV) by

gesting that the HB-associated self-assembled ordered interlayer indeed

dopants (e.g., tBP and LiTFSI) migration[39] towards the perovskite| 
HTM interface. We evaluated the long-term shelf stability by comparing

material (O1) that, while acting as HTM in PSCs, can self-assemble via 
hydrogen bonding into an interlayer at the perovskite|HTM interface. 
We also studied a reference material (O2), similar to O1 in the molecular 
structure except for the replacement of the HB-forming unit (butana­
mide) in O1 with a plain butyl chain. Our experimental and theoretical 
results suggest that O1 has higher hole mobility than O2 and induces a 
better energy level alignment with the VB of perovskite, due to the 
formation of a supramolecular structure via intermolecular hydrogen 
bonds within the O1 HTM. More importantly, the presence of a HB- 
directed long-range ordered interlayer leads to an efficient hole 
extraction process and suppression of interfacial charge recombination 
because of the effectively reduced hole trap density on the perovskite 
surface. This is evident by the 60 mV Voc enhancement, the > 11% FF 
increase, as well as the reduced hysteresis in the J–V curves of O1-based 
devices vs. the O2-based counterparts. The O1-based n-i-p type PSCs with 
no encapsulation demonstrate high air stability after ~100 h under 
continuous MPPT with an extracted T80 of 35.5 h, which is nearly one 
order of magnitude longer than that (3.7 h) obtained for O2-based de­
vices. By proposing a material (O1) that combines the hole transport 
function with the capability of modifying the perovskite interface by 
self-assembling into an ordered interlayer, we believe our work will 
pave the way for further HTM design modifications for efficient and 
stable n-i-p PSCs.
